paragraphs.content:
Substations and parking garages are examples of industrial occupancies
where staff presence may be permanent or may be intermittent. In the
case of parking garages, the presence of occupants other than staff
is transitory.

[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect7.subsect2.art2.sent1:long] assumes that there will be a sufficient number
of persons in the building to justify the provision of separate water
closet facilities for both males and females. In some circumstances
overall low occupant loads would not require more than one water closet
for males and one water closet for females and yet the building has
more than one storey. It is deemed that rooms each containing a single
water closet available for both males and females would satisfy the
intent of the Code. The total number of water closets must be adequate
for the total number of occupants. Requirements for barrier free accessibility
also need to be considered. If the entrance storey is accessible and
the upper storeys are not required to be accessible, a room in the
accessible storey must meet the requirements of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8:long] and can serve both males and females. If provided,
a nonaccessible room, designed to serve both males and females, in
each nonaccessible upper storey would be acceptable. [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect7.subsect2.art2.sent2:long] permits a single water closet to serve both males
and females if the total occupant load is low.

This Section contains minimum requirements for the design of buildings that accommodate
people with diverse abilities, across their lifespan, including, but
not limited to, people who use wheelchairs or other assistive mobility
devices (e.g., walking aids, canes, crutches, braces, prosthetics),
people with personal care providers, people with hearing or vision
loss, and people with service animals, so they can access and use
buildings.

Examples of basic accessibility requirements of the Code are as follows: 
                        a clear floor space of at least 800 mm (metric) by 1 350 mm (metric),
                        a 1 000 mm (metric) clear width allowing a 90° turn, 
                        a 2 100 mm (metric) diameter clear floor space allowing
a 180° turn in one motion, and
                        a 1 700 mm (metric) diameter clear floor space allowing
a 180° turn in multiple motions.

Industrial
buildings often pose a greater risk to their occupants due to the
presence of significant quantities of dangerous materials or the use
of hazardous processes. For example, plants which are classified as
Group F, Division 2 or 3, may store and use toxic or highly flammable
substances in significant quantities, or house processes which involve
very high temperatures and which have a high degree of automation.
In some facilities, particularly in primary industries such as forestry
and metallurgy, the construction normally used and the operations
carried out within the space can make compliance with the requirements
of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8:long] impracticable. It is therefore intended
that these requirements be applied with discretion in buildings of
Group F, Division 2 or 3 major occupancy. However, where industrial
buildings contain subsidiary occupancies, such as offices or showrooms,
it is reasonable to require that accessibility be provided in these
spaces.

An accessible
route should exist from the sidewalk or roadway and parking area to
an accessible building entrance. This route should be located so that people do not have to
pass behind parked cars.

[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art2:long] applies to all entrances, including public and
employee entrances, that provide access to a barrier-free storey.
Doors that open onto exterior facilities that are only accessible
from inside the building (e.g., hotel pools) are not considered entrances
in the context of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art2:long]

If barrier-free access is required into suites or rooms in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2:long], it is intended that access be provided, with
some exceptions identified in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.sent2:long], throughout each room or suite. Some examples of
where barrier-free access is required are as follows:
                        within each suite (subject to [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.sent2.clause11:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.sent2.clause12:short]),
                        within rooms or areas that serve the public or are designated
for use by visitors, including areas in assembly occupancies with
fixed seats, display areas and merchandising departments,
                        within rooms or areas for student use in assembly occupancies,
                        within general work areas, including office areas,
                        within general use or general service areas, including shared
laundry areas in residential occupancies, recreational areas, cafeterias,
lounge rooms, lunch rooms and infirmaries,
                        within sleeping rooms in hospitals and nursing homes with
treatment,
                        (if installed), into at least one passenger elevator or
elevating device conforming to [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect5.subsect2.art1:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art7:long],
                        into washrooms described in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art8.sent1:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art8.sent4:short], 
                        to any facility required by this Section to be designed
to accommodate persons with physical disabilities,
                        onto every balcony provided in conformance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect3.subsect1.art7.sent1.clause3:long], and
                        to service counters used by the general public (examples
include ticket counters, refreshment stands, drinking fountains, cafeteria
counters, checkout counters and bank service counters).

The permission to waive a barrier-free path of travel for wheelchair
access to certain specified areas of a building is not intended to
waive accessibility requirements for persons whose physical disabilities
do not require special provision for access to raised or sunken levels.
Persons with visual or hearing disabilities that do not require the
use of a wheelchair can be expected to move throughout a building.

Seating booths and banquettes in restaurants and bars are considered
furniture, which is beyond the scope of the Code. However, various
types of seating should be considered to ensure the availability of
barrier-free options.

The concept of wheelchair accessibility does not
extend to building service facilities, nor to all floor levels within
a storey, e.g., mezzanines not served by an elevator. Mezzanines that
are accessible by an elevator are therefore not excluded.

application_notes.title:
Access to Facilities on a Floor
Level other than the Entrance Level

paragraphs.content:
[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.sent2.clause7.subclause2:long]
                     [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.sent2.clause7.subclause4:shortSbcl] are intended to exempt certain
storeys other than the entrance level—including basements and mezzanines
that are less than 600 m2
                      (metric) in floor area
or 100 m2
                      (metric) or less in floor area in assembly
occupancies, that are self-contained, or that contain the same facilities
as the entrance level— from the requirement to have a barrier-free
path of travel. Examples of buildings and spaces to which this exemption
may apply are small office buildings with additional workspaces on
the second storey and small restaurants with a second storey that
contains only additional seating. However, if a restaurant's
only washrooms are in the basement, they must have a barrier-free
path of travel as they are an integral part of the principal function
of the first storey. Similarly, staff lunchrooms and washrooms are
also integral to the principal function of a restaurant; as such,
if they are located in a floor area such as a second storey, basement
or mezzanine that contains essential facilities as described in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.sent2.clause7.subclause3:long], they must have a barrier-free path of travel
for potential employees with disabilities.

Where a building contains more than one floor level, other than
the entrance level, each floor level should be considered individually
when determining the floor area for the purposes of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.sent2.clause7.subclause2:long]
                     [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.sent2.clause7.subclause4:shortSbcl]. Mezzanines should be considered
as a floor level other than the entrance level.

Many types of buildings have waiting areas, such as airports,
hospitals, and government office buildings. Waiting areas should have
a sufficient number of spaces designated for persons using wheelchairs
so they can use the waiting area without blocking any means of egress.

The number of people using wheelchairs is typically much higher
in treatment occupancies than in other types of occupancies. Designers
should consider adding more designated wheelchair spaces in waiting
areas than the numbers indicated in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art3.table1:long] in
occupancies where a higher number of persons using wheelchairs is
expected due to the types of services provided.

application_notes.title:
Distribution of Adaptable Seats, Designated Wheelchair Spaces, and
Mobility Aid Storage Spaces in Assembly Occupancies

figures.title:
Example of distribution of adaptable
seats, designated wheelchair spaces, and mobility aid storage spaces
in an auditorium

graphic.alt_text: Example of distribution of adaptable seats, designated wheelchair spaces, and mobility aid storage spaces in an auditorium

application_notes.title:
Access to Storeys Served by Escalators
and Moving Walks

paragraphs.content:
In some buildings, escalators and inclined
moving walks are installed to provide transportation from one floor
level to another floor level so as to increase the capacity to move
large numbers of persons. Some buildings located on a sloping site
are accessible from street level on more than one storey and an escalator
or inclined moving walk is provided for internal movement from floor
to floor. In both these situations, people must be provided with an
equally convenient means of moving between the same floor levels within
the building. This may be accomplished by providing elevators, platform-equipped
passenger-elevating devices, or ramps, for example.

In localities
where local regulations or bylaws do not govern the provision of or
dimensions of barrier-free parking spaces, the following provides
guidance to determine appropriate provisions. If more than 50 parking
spaces are provided, parking spaces for use by persons with physical
disabilities should be provided in the ratio of one for every 100
parking spaces or part thereof. Parking spaces for use by persons
with physical disabilities should
                        be not less than 2 400 mm (metric) wide and provided
on one side with an access aisle not less than 1 500 mm (metric) wide,
                        have a firm, slip-resistant and level surface,
                        be located close to an entrance required to conform to [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art2:long],
                        be clearly marked as being for the use of persons with physical
disabilities, and
                        be identified by a sign located not less than 1 500
mm (metric) above ground level, with the International Symbol of Access
and the words “Permit Required” ([REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote189.figure1:long]).

Asphalt, concrete and gravel are acceptable parking surfaces.
Curb ramps should be not less than 920 mm (metric) wide. Parallel
parking spaces should be not less than 7 000 mm (metric) long.
If more than one parking space is provided for persons with physical
disabilities, a single access aisle can serve two adjacent parking
spaces. The arrangement shown in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote189.figure2:long] allows
the shared use of an access aisle to serve two adjacent parking spaces
provided for use by persons with physical disabilities.

figures.title:
“Permit Required”
sign

graphic.alt_text: “Permit Required” sign

figures.title: Shared access aisle

graphic.alt_text: Shared access aisle

paragraphs.content:
The intent of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art5.sent1:long]
                     [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art5.sent2:short] is to ensure that exterior barrier-free paths of travel are readily
available so that persons of all abilities can move to and from a
building with minimal effort and in a manner that minimizes the total
distance required to be travelled.

[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art6.sent1:long] is not intended to
reduce the functionality of security devices that limit access to
secure areas and are addressed by other Sections of the NBC.

application_notes.title:
Power Door Operators for Interior
Doors

paragraphs.content:
It is not intended that all doors located in a
barrier-free path of travel be equipped with a power door operator,
but rather those that are located within public areas of the building,
such as public corridors or corridors used by the public. Doors of
suites served by a public area do not need to be equipped with a power
door operator.

In selecting which doorway to equip with a power
door operator as required by [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art7.sent3:long], consideration
should be given to the location of barrier-free paths of travel, to
the ease of access, and to minimizing congestion.

A universal washroom is an accessible space providing
privacy for one person and their care attendant(s), regardless of
their gender. It is intended that a universal washroom be available
in close proximity to each bank of washrooms in a floor area. In the
case where only one water closet is provided, a universal washroom
would satisfy the requirement of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art8.sent1:long].

[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote194.figure1:long] presents examples
of washroom floor plan combinations that include men's, women's, accessible
and universal washrooms.

figures.title:
Washroom floor plan
options that include accessible and universal washrooms

graphic.alt_text: Washroom floor plan options that include accessible and universal washrooms

paragraphs.content:
A universal dressing and shower room is a barrier-free
space that contains a shower and a space for dressing for one person
and their care attendant(s) and provides privacy, regardless of gender.

It is intended that a universal dressing and shower room be
available within close proximity to each bank of showers in a floor
area. In cases where only one shower is provided, a universal dressing
and shower room would satisfy the requirement.

The intent of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art8.sent15:long] is to ensure that
in large major occupancies, such as large shopping malls, public pools
and libraries, occupants who may need assistance with personal hygiene
will have access to an accessible change space that can be found in
a consistent location.

Universal washrooms containing an accessible change space should
be located so that they are available to the public when the large
major occupancy is occupied. A suitable location could be in the lobby
of a building housing the large major occupancy that remains open
during that major occupancy's business hours, for example.

application_notes.title:
Assistive Listening Systems and
Adaptive Technologies

paragraphs.content:
The intent of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect2.art9.sent2:long] is to require that at least one counter with an
assistive listening system or adaptive technology be provided at each
group of service counters providing the same exchange of information,
goods or services. For example, in a stadium with ticket counters
at multiple building entrances, at least one ticket counter at each
entrance should be equipped with an assistive listening system or
adaptive technology.

The NBC requires that directional signs be provided in a number of
situations. Although they are only required to provide visual information,
tactile directional signs should also be provided where practicable.

In some buildings, it may be necessary to supplement signs that
provide visual and tactile information with visual displays, such
as information displays and electronic interactive displays (e.g.,
wayfinding, exhibits and self-serve points-of-sale). Visual displays
are common in motion picture theatres, law courts, exhibition halls,
passenger stations/depots, museums, conference facilities, shops,
stores and markets.

Wherever practicable, visual displays should be designed so
that they are accessible to all people. In order to be accessible
to people with low vision, visually displayed information should also
be audibly communicated, either electronically or orally. Where touch
screens are installed, an alternative means of accessing the information
should be provided, for example by providing tactile buttons on an
interactive display or by ensuring an attendant is always available
to assist customers or visitors. Visual displays should also be accessible
to people who use mobility devices. The degree of operability should
accommodate people using a wide range of mobility devices (e.g., wheelchairs,
scooters, walkers, canes) and people with a wide range of arm and
hand mobility. Approach side, mounting height above the finished floor,
amount of knee space, types of controls and the ability to reach them
are particularly important considerations.

It is not intended that all counters be barrier-free, but that
sufficient barrier-free counter space be available. Examples of counters
that should be barrier-free include check-in counters and those in
financial institutions and reception areas as well as any counter
at which processing and signing of documents takes place. The provision
is not intended to apply to work surfaces in industrial occupancies.

Code users who opt to apply the provisions of [REF:standard:csab651] listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art1.table1:long] must do so without exception: they cannot randomly
select and apply a mix of provisions from the NBC and that standard.

Reduction in Clear Width of Barrier-Free
Path of Travel

paragraphs.content:

schematic examples of barrier-free paths of travel with a section
whose clear width is reduced as permitted by [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art2.sent2:long].

Barrier-free paths of travel with a

application_notes.title:
Surfaces in a Barrier-free Path
of Travel

paragraphs.content:
Floor finishes, including walk-off matts and
carpet, should be selected, installed and securely fixed to provide
a firm and stable surface so that people, including those who use mobility
aids, can easily travel over them without tripping or expending undue
energy. Other than very high-density, short-pile carpeting, most carpeting
does not meet these criteria.

Furthermore, where the path of travel is exposed to intense
light conditions, such as daylight or directional lighting, a low-glare
or matte floor surface should be selected, as glare from floor surfaces
can influence all users' perception, particularly those with vision loss. For the same reasons, heavily patterned flooring should also be
avoided.

[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art2.sent6:long] presents three options
for the design of clear floor spaces at the end of long narrow sections
of barrier-free paths of travel to allow persons using a wheelchair
to turn around instead of having to back up.

[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote203.figure1:long] illustrates one possible configuration
of a T-shaped wheelchair-turning space.

figures.title: T-shaped wheelchair-turning space

graphic.alt_text: T-shaped wheelchair-turning space

paragraphs.content:
Ramps
with a slope of more than 1 in 16 can be very difficult for persons
with physical disabilities with upper body mobility to manage. Even
though they pose less of a problem for persons in motorized wheelchairs,
these ramps can be unsafe to descend, especially in cold climates.
Although [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art5:long] permits slopes
on ramps as great as 1 in 12 for distances of up to 9 m (metric), slopes of 1 in 20 are safer and less strenuous. When limited space
is available, as may be the case during renovations, ramps with a
slope of up to 1 in 12 should be restricted to lengths not exceeding 3 m (metric) whenever possible. A strip contrasting in colour and texture
should be used at the top and bottom of ramps to warn persons with
low or no vision.

The phrase “uniform slope along its length” is intended to mean that
the slope remains constant along the length of individual ramp segments.

application_notes.title:
Landing Design at Doorways Leading
to Ramps

figures.title:
Landing design at
doorways leading to ramps

graphic.alt_text: Landing design at doorways leading to ramps

paragraphs.content:
[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art2.sent3:long] requires that all walking surfaces in
a barrier-free path of travel be stable and firm to limit the effort
required by persons using wheelchairs or other mobility aids. Therefore, [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art5.sent4:long] requires that hard or resilient flooring be used
on the surfaces of steeper ramps. Furthermore, carpet and like materials
should not be installed on any ramp.

Standard
wheelchair width specifications indicate a range of sizes from 584 mm (metric) overall to 685 mm (metric) overall. Every doorway
that is located in a barrier-free path of travel must have a clear
width of not less than 850 mm (metric) when the door
is in the open position and therefore it is important that this dimension
be measured correctly. [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote207.figure1:long] shows a door
opened to 90° (metric). It is clear that the door, and to a lesser
extent the stop, impinges on the space within the door frame. The
clear width of not less than 850 mm (metric) is measured
from the face of the door to the outside edge of the stop on the door
frame. It is not sufficient just to measure the inside width of the
door frame. Other factors should be taken into account, including the location
of door stops other than on the door frame, and the installation of
door closers and exit devices, even if they do not span the width
of the entire door. The intrusion of a door handle into
the space is of lesser importance. It is recognized that there are
many types of door frames and door mounts, but the overall objective
is to maintain a clear width of not less than 850 mm (metric).

The diagram depicts a somewhat restrictive scenario, as many
doors can open wider than  90° (metric) to ensure the minimum clear width of 850 mm (metric) that is required.

figures.title: Clear doorway width

graphic.alt_text: Clear doorway width

paragraphs.content:
This requirement ensures that the doorway to the washroom in
a dwelling unit or a hotel or motel suite is at least large enough
to accommodate someone using a wheelchair. The Code does not require
these washrooms to be barrier-free, in order to avoid a set of prescriptive
requirements which could limit design flexibility. It is relatively
simple to make washrooms accessible through careful planning and positioning
of fixtures and this can be achieved in an area not much larger than
that of conventional washrooms.

figures.title: Residential washrooms

graphic.alt_text: Residential washrooms

paragraphs.content:
Lever
handles are usable by most people and will meet the intent of this
requirement. Lever handles with an end return towards the door are
less prone to catch the clothing of someone passing through the doorway.

Doors equipped with a power operator actuated by a pressure
plate identified with the International Symbol of Access or, where
security is required, by a key, card or radio transmitter, and that
can otherwise be opened manually, meet the intent of the requirement.
The location of these actuating devices should ensure that a wheelchair
will not interfere with the operation of the door once it is actuated.
Swinging doors equipped with power operators which are actuated automatically
and open into passing pedestrian traffic should be provided with a
guard or other device designed to prevent pedestrians from stepping
in the swing area of the door. These guards or devices should be detectable
by blind persons. For example, inverted U-shaped guards should have
an additional rail at a height not more than 680 mm (metric) so
that it is detectable by the long cane. These doors should also have
a device (mat or other sensor) on the swing side to prevent the door
from opening if someone is standing in the swing area.

Differences in air pressure on opposite sides of a door may
be due to the operation of mechanical systems such as those associated
with smoke control. So-called “stack action” in buildings in winter
can also cause differential pressures due to the buoyancy of warm
air. Stack action is usually most noticeable between stairwells and
the remainder of the building, and at the entrances to buildings;
the taller the building, the greater the effect. Doors with automatic
closers have to operate with sufficient opening force to allow the
return action to overcome the differential pressure.

In some circumstances, closers with a delay feature which keeps
the door open for several seconds before it begins to close might
be desirable. However, closers with this feature have limited back-check,
a feature of a normal door closer where resistance to opening increases
as the door reaches the full arc of swing. Doors equipped with a delayed
action closer are therefore more susceptible to damage should the
door be opened with too much force or should someone try to force
it closed, thinking the closer has failed to operate. Delayed action
closers are not recommended for such occupancies as schools.

Sufficient clearance must be provided on the latch side of doors
for a user to operate the door-opening mechanism and open the door
without interference from the wheelchair. This is particularly important
for a door swinging towards the approach side. See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote213.figure1:long].

graphic.alt_text: Doorway clearance

Minimum Clear Floor Space

paragraphs.content:
In the
context of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art6.sent17:long], “public area” is intended
to refer to a suite, room or area that is generally open to building
occupants, such as a cafeteria, lounge room, washroom or office, but
is not intended to include a space such as a janitor's room,
service space or service room.

Security access systems are a typical example of systems that
have controls that provide feedback signals, such as illumination
and an audible cue, which should be accessible to all users.

figures.title:
Positioning of visual and tactile information
signs on and near doors

graphic.alt_text: Positioning of visual and tactile information signs on and near doors

paragraphs.content:
The International Symbol of Access shown in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote218.figure1:long] indicates to persons with physical disabilities that they will
have reasonable freedom of movement within a building so signed. The
symbol is usually white on a blue background; where these colours
do not stand out, the sign can be set on a white background. An arrow
can be added to indicate direction or the location of an accessible
space or facility.

The International Symbol of Access for Hearing Loss shown in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote218.figure2:long], which indicates accessibility for persons with
hearing loss, should be used to indicate the availability of variable
volume controls on telephones, assistive listening systems, and text
telephones (TT). These latter devices may also be referred to as teletypewriters
(TTY) or telecommunications devices for the deaf (TDD).

Signs indicating accessible
facilities

Signs for assistive
listening facilities

application_notes.title:
Lateral Transfer Space on Alternate
Sides of Water Closet

paragraphs.content:
The lateral transfer space required
by [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art12.sent1.clause2:long] should be provided on the right side
in one accessible stall or universal washroom and on the left side
in another so that users can choose the facility with a transfer space
on the side they prefer to use.

Doors to water-closet stalls for persons with physical disabilities
should swing outward, preferably against a side wall.

figures.title:
Water-closet
stalls

graphic.alt_text: Water-closet stalls

paragraphs.content:
The door pull should consist of a D-shaped handle mounted horizontally.
The centre lines are the lines drawn through the long axis and the
short axis of the handle. The midpoint of the handle must be located
horizontally at 200 to 300 mm (metric) from the hinged side of
the door and vertically at 800 to 1 000 mm (metric) above the
finished floor surface.

paragraphs.content:
It is the designer's prerogative to exceed the minimum requirements
found in the NBC and specify the installation of additional grab bars
in other locations. These additional grab bars may be of different
configurations and can be installed in other orientations.

application_notes.title: Clear Floor Space in Universal Washrooms

paragraphs.content:
Unobstructed areas in front of the lavatory, in front of the
water closet and on one side of the water closet are necessary for
maneuverability of a wheelchair. Although outward swinging doors are
preferable for accessibility, inward swinging doors are also permitted. [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote224.figure1:long]
                     [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote224.figure2:long] show design options that meet the intent of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art13:long]

paragraphs.content:
Wall-
or floor-mounted water closets with recessed bases are preferable
because they provide the least amount of obstruction.

figures.title:
Clearances beneath
a lavatory

graphic.alt_text: Clearances beneath a lavatory

paragraphs.content:
The pipes referred to in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art16.sent1.clause6:long] include both
supply and waste pipes. The hazard can be prevented by insulating
the pipes, by locating the pipes in enclosures, or avoided by limiting
the temperature of the hot water to a maximum of 45°C (metric).

The location of accessories, such as soap dispensers and faucets,
serving barrier-free lavatories should be established while taking
into consideration that their controls must be usable by and within
the direct reach of a person in a seated position directly in front
of the accessible lavatory.

application_notes.title:
Clear Space at Entrances to
Showers

paragraphs.content:
The clear space at the entrance to a shower may
be encroached upon by fixtures such as a wall hung sink which does
not interfere with the leg rests of the wheelchair. However, this
sink could restrict movement for persons who need to make a lateral
transfer if it were installed at the seat end of the shower.

figures.title: Shower design

graphic.alt_text: Shower design

paragraphs.content:
One
L-shaped grab bar is required to be installed on the wall next to
the seat. A grab bar behind the seat would prevent the user from leaning
back against the wall, while one located on the wall opposite the
seat cannot be reached from the seated position. The seat itself may
be used in conjunction with the bar for transfer. If design flexibility
is required, fold away grab bars can be used as an alternative.

Where a bench in a universal dressing and shower room is located
adjacent to a wall, it is recommended that a grab bar be installed
to assist users in transferring to the bench.

Examples of assistive
listening systems include FM, infrared and induction loop systems.
However, the technology in this field is advancing rapidly; as such,
other types of assistive listening systems could be considered in
the design of a space. In choosing the most appropriate system, a
number of factors must be taken into account including cost, installation
and maintenance requirements, suitability for the intended user or
audience, ease of operation, and the need for privacy. Information
on designers and suppliers of such systems can be obtained from the
Canadian Hearing Society. The intent of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art19:long] is to provide clear communication where information, goods or services
are provided to the public.

Wireless sound transmission systems, including
FM, infrared and magnetic induction loop systems, improve sound reception
for persons who are hard
of hearing by providing amplification that can be adjusted by each
user while blocking out unwanted background noise. Some of these systems
transmit a signal that is picked up by a special receiver (FM, infrared)
available for use by a person who is hard of hearing, whether or not
a hearing aid is used. None of the systems interfere with
the listening enjoyment of others.

The transmitter can be connected into an existing public address (P.A.) system amplifier
or used independently with microphones. The induction loop system
(see [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote232.figure3:long]) requires users with a hearing
aid or cochlear implant to be in the area circumscribed
by the loop; though installation of the loop is relatively simple,
the installer should be knowledgeable about these systems if proper
functioning is to be achieved. FM and infrared systems can be designed
to broadcast signals that cover the entire room and thus do not restrict
seating to any one area. [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote232.figure1:long]
                     [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect9.appnote232.figure2:long] show the general configuration
of FM and infrared systems. Although portable systems (FM systems,
in particular) are available, these are best suited to small audiences.
Generally, the systems installed in church halls, auditoria, theatres
and similar places of assembly are not easily portable, as they are
installed in a fixed location by a sound technician and form an integral
part of the P.A. system of the room or building.

Hard-wired systems (where a connection is provided at a particular seat in an
auditorium, for example) might meet this requirement when adequate provisions are made to accommodate persons with hearing
aids.

paragraphs.content:
Where forward-facing interaction with a person is required,
the knee space requirement of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art20.sent1.clause3:long] applies
to both sides of the service counter to ensure accessibility for both
service providers and those receiving services.

Built-in shelves or counters for public telephones must be designed
to accommodate persons using text telephones (TT). These devices may
also be referred to as teletypewriters (TTY) or telecommunication
devices for the deaf (TDD). These devices require a level surface
at least 305 mm (metric) deep by 250 mm (metric) wide with
no obstruction above that space within 250 mm (metric). If a wall-hung
telephone or other obstruction extends to less than 250 mm (metric) from the shelf or counter, an equivalent clear space must be provided
on either side of each telephone. At least one telephone should be
equipped with a volume control on a receiver that generates a magnetic
field compatible with the T-switch of a hearing aid. The lower portion
of the shelf or counter is intended for persons using a wheelchair;
therefore all parts of the operating mechanism of the telephone above
this portion should be within reach of a wheelchair user.

The intent of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part3.sect8.subsect3.art22.sent4:long] is that a sufficient
number of storage spaces for mobility aids other than wheelchairs
and scooters (e.g., walkers) be located such that they can be accessed
without leaving the seating area. These storage spaces should preferably
be visible from the adaptable seats. The storage spaces may be located
adjacent to an aisle but must not reduce the required egress width
of the aisle or obstruct egress from the rows of seats.

content.text: The scope of this Part shall be as described in [REF:internal:nbc.divA.part1.sect3.subsect3:long].
Words that appear in italics in this Part are defined in [REF:internal:nbc.divA.part1.sect4.subsect1.art2:long].

[REF:term:bldng]Buildings and their structural members
and connections, including formwork and falsework, shall be designed
to have sufficient structural capacity and structural integrity to
safely and effectively resist all loads, effects of loads and influences
that may reasonably be expected, having regard to the expected service
life of [REF:term:bldng]buildings, and shall in any case
satisfy the requirements of this Section. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote1:short].)

[REF:term:bldng]Buildings and their structural members
shall be designed for serviceability, in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art4:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art5:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art6:long] (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote2:short].)

All permanent and temporary structural members, including the
formwork and falsework of a [REF:term:bldng]building, shall
be protected against loads exceeding the specified loads during the
construction period except when, as verified by analysis or test,
temporary overloading of a structural member would result in no impairment
of that member or any other member.

Falsework, scaffolding, and formwork shall be designed in conformance
with

clauses.text: [REF:standard:csas269.1]
[REF:standard:csas269.2] or
[REF:standard:csas269.3]

content.text:
Precautions shall be taken during all phases of construction
to ensure that the [REF:term:bldng]building is not damaged
or distorted due to loads applied during construction.

Structural drawings and related documents shall conform to the
appropriate requirements of [REF:internal:nbc.divC.part2.sect2:long]. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divC.part2.sect2.subsect4:long].)

Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect1.art5.sent2:short], [REF:term:bldng]buildings and their structural members
shall be designed in conformance with the procedures and practices
provided in this Part.

Provided the design is carried out by a person especially qualified
in the specific methods applied and provided the design demonstrates
a level of safety and performance in accordance with the requirements
of Part 4, [REF:term:bldng]buildings and their structural
components falling within the scope of Part 4 that are not amenable
to analysis using a generally established theory may be designed by

clauses.text:
evaluation of a full-scale structure or a prototype by a loading
test, or
studies of model analogues.

content.text:
Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect2.art2:long], the following
categories of loads, specified loads and effects shall be taken into
consideration in the design of a [REF:term:bldng]building and its structural members and connections:

D[REF:term:dd-ld]dead load –
a permanent load due to the weight of [REF:term:bldng]building components, as specified in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect4:long],


Eearthquake load and effects – a rare load
due to an earthquake, as specified in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect8:long],


Ha permanent load due to lateral earth pressure,
including [REF:term:grndwtr]groundwater,


L[REF:term:lv-ld]live load –
a variable load due to intended use and [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy (including loads due to cranes and the pressure of liquids in containers),
as specified in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5:long],


L_{XC}
                           [REF:term:lv-ld]live load exclusive of crane loads,


C[REF:term:lv-ld]live load due
to cranes including self weight,


C_{d}self weight of all cranes positioned
for maximum effects,


C_{7}crane bumper impact load,


Ppermanent effects caused by pre-stress,


Svariable load due to snow, including ice
and associated rain, as specified in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2:long],
or due to rain, as specified in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art4:long],


Teffects due to contraction, expansion,
or deflection caused by temperature changes, shrinkage, moisture changes,
creep, ground settlement, or a combination thereof (see [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote5:short]), and


Wwind load – a variable load due to wind,
as specified in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect7:long],

where

clauses.text:
load means the imposed deformations (i.e. deflections, displacements
or motions that induce deformations and forces in the structure),
forces and pressures applied to the [REF:term:bldng]building structure,

permanent load is a load that changes very little once it has
been applied to the structure, except during repair,

variable load is a load that frequently changes in magnitude,
direction or location, and

rare load is a load that occurs infrequently and for a short
time only.

content.text:
Minimum specified values of the loads described in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect2.art1.sent1:short], as set forth in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect4:long] to [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect8:number], shall be increased to account
for dynamic effects where applicable.

For the purpose of determining specified loads S, W or E in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect7:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect8:long], [REF:term:bldng]buildings shall be assigned an Importance
Category based on intended use and [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy, in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect2.art1.table1:long] (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote6:short].)

content.title: Importance Categories for BuildingsSee [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote7:short]

body_rows.content:
A Low Importance Category [REF:term:bldng]building is a [REF:term:bldng]building that represents a low direct
or indirect hazard to human life in the event of structural failure.

A Normal Importance Category [REF:term:bldng]building is a [REF:term:bldng]building that does
not meet the criteria for a Low Importance Category [REF:term:bldng]building, High Importance Category [REF:term:bldng]building or [REF:term:pt-dtr-b]post-disaster building.

A High Importance Category [REF:term:bldng]building is a [REF:term:bldng]building that provides a greater
degree of safety to human life than a Normal Importance Category [REF:term:bldng]building. Community centres and elementary, middle
and secondary schools are High Importance Category [REF:term:bldng]buildings.

content.text:
Where a [REF:term:bldng]building or structural member
can be expected to be subjected to loads, forces or other effects
not listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect2.art1:long], such effects shall be taken
into account in the design based on the most appropriate information
available. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote8:short].)
In this Subsection, the term

clauses.text:
limit states means those conditions of a [REF:term:bldng]building structure that result in the [REF:term:bldng]building ceasing to fulfill the function for which it was
designed (those limit states concerning safety are called ultimate
limit states (ULS) and include exceeding the load-carrying capacity,
overturning, sliding and fracture; those limit states that restrict
the intended use and [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy of the [REF:term:bldng]building are called serviceability limit states
(SLS) and include deflection, vibration, permanent deformation and
local structural damage such as cracking; and those limit states that
represent failure under repeated loading are called fatigue limit
states),

specified loads (C, D, E, H, L, P, S, T and W) means those loads
defined in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect2.art1:long],

principal load means the specified variable load or rare load
that dominates in a given load combination,

companion load means a specified variable load that accompanies
the principal load in a given load combination,

service load means a specified load used for the evaluation
of a serviceability limit state,

principal-load factor means a factor applied to the principal
load in a load combination to account for the variability of the load
and load pattern and the analysis of its effects,

companion-load factor means a factor that, when applied to a
companion load in the load combination, gives the probable magnitude
of a companion load acting simultaneously with the factored principal
load,

importance factor, I, means a factor applied in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6:long]
                              [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect7:long]
                              [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect8:long] to obtain the specified load and take into account the consequences
of failure as related to the limit state and the use and [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy of the [REF:term:bldng]building,

factored load means the product of a specified load and its
principal-load factor or companion-load factor,

effects refers to forces, moments, deformations or vibrations
that occur in the structure,

nominal resistance, R, of a member, connection or structure,
is based on the geometry and on the specified properties of the structural
materials,

resistance factor, φ, means a factor applied to a specified
material property or to the resistance of a member, connection or
structure, and that, for the limit state under consideration, takes
into account the variability of dimensions and material properties,
workmanship, type of failure and uncertainty in the prediction of
resistance, and

factored resistance, φR, means the product of nominal resistance
and the applicable resistance factor.

content.text:
A [REF:term:bldng]building and its structural components
shall be designed to have sufficient strength and stability so that
the factored resistance, φR, is greater than or equal to the effect
of factored loads, which shall be determined in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.sent2:short].

Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.sent3:short], the effect of factored loads for a [REF:term:bldng]building or structural component shall be determined in accordance with the
requirements of this Article and the following load combination cases,
the applicable combination being that which results in the most critical
effect:

clauses.text:
for load cases without crane loads, the load combinations listed
in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table1:long], and

for load cases with crane loads, the load combinations listed
in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table2:long].

content.text:
Other load combinations that must also be considered are the
principal loads acting with the companion loads taken as zero.

Where the effects due to lateral earth pressure, H, restraint
effects from pre-stress, P, and imposed deformation, T, affect the
structural safety, they shall be taken into account in the calculations,
with load factors of 1.5, 1.0 and 1.25 assigned to H, P and T respectively.
(See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote11:short].)

Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect8.art16.sent2:long], the counteracting
factored [REF:term:dd-ld]dead load—0.9D in load combination
cases 2, 3 and 4 and 1.0D in load combination case 5 in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table1:long], and 0.9D in load combination cases 1 to 5 and
1.0D in load combination case 6 in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table2:long]—shall
be used when the [REF:term:dd-ld]dead load acts to resist
overturning, uplift, sliding, failure due to stress reversal, and
to determine anchorage requirements and the factored resistance of
members. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote12:short].)

The principal-load factor 1.5 for [REF:term:lv-ld]live loads L in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table1:long] and L_{XC} in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table2:long] may be reduced to 1.25 for liquids in tanks.

The companion-load factor for [REF:term:lv-ld]live loads L in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table1:long] and L_{XC} in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table2:long] shall be increased by 0.5 for storage areas, and
equipment areas and [REF:term:rvc-rm]service rooms referred
to in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art3.table1:long]

content.title:
Load Combinations Without Crane Loads for Ultimate Limit
States
Load Combinations With Crane Loads for Ultimate Limit States

content.text:
Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.sent9:short], the load factor 1.25 for [REF:term:dd-ld]dead load,
D, for [REF:term:l]soil, superimposed earth, plants and
trees given in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table1:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table2:long] shall be increased to 1.5, except
that when the [REF:term:l]soil depth exceeds 1.2
m (metric), the factor may be reduced to 1 + 0.6/h_{s} but not
less than 1.25, where h_{s} is the depth of [REF:term:l]soil, in m, supported by the structure.

A principal-load factor of 1.5 shall be applied to the weight
of saturated [REF:term:l]soil used in load combination
case 1 of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table1:long].

Earthquake load, E, in load combination cases 5 of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table1:long] and 6 of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2.table2:long] includes horizontal
earth pressure due to earthquake determined in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect8.art16.sent7:long].

Provision shall be made to ensure adequate stability of the
structure as a whole and adequate lateral, torsional and local stability
of all structural parts.

Sway effects produced by vertical loads acting on the structure
in its displaced configuration shall be taken into account in the
design of [REF:term:bldng]buildings and their structural
members.

A [REF:term:bldng]building and its structural components,
including connections, shall be checked for fatigue failure under
the effect of cyclical loads, as required in the standards listed
in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect3:long] (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote13:short].)

Where vibration effects, such as resonance and fatigue resulting
from machinery and equipment, are likely to be significant, a dynamic
analysis shall be carried out. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote14:short].)

A [REF:term:bldng]building and its structural components
shall be checked for serviceability limit states as defined in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art1.sent1.clause1:long] under the effect of service loads for serviceability
criteria specified or recommended in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art5:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art6:long] and in
the standards listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect3:long] (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote15:short].)

The effect of service loads on the serviceability limit states
shall be determined in accordance with this Article and the load combinations
listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art4.table1:long], the applicable combination
being that which results in the most critical effect.

Other load combinations that must also be considered are the
principal loads acting with the companion loads taken as zero.

Deflections calculated for load types P, T and H, if present,
with load factors of 1.0 shall be included with the calculated deflections
due to principal loads.
The determination of the deflection shall consider the following:

clauses.text:
for materials that result in increased deformations over time
under sustained loads, the deflection calculation shall consider the
portion of [REF:term:lv-ld]live load, L, that is sustained
over time, L_{s}, and the portion that is transitory, L_{t}, and

the calculated deflection due to [REF:term:dd-ld]dead load, D, and sustained [REF:term:lv-ld]live load, L_{s}, shall be increased by a creep factor as specified in the standards
listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect3:long] to obtain the additional long-term
deflection.

content.text: The determination of the long-term settlement of [REF:term:fndtn]foundations shall consider the following:

clauses.text:
for [REF:term:fndtn]foundation
                              [REF:term:l]soil types that result in increased settlement over time under sustained
loads, the additional long-term settlements shall be determined for
the portion of [REF:term:lv-ld]live load, L, that is sustained
over time, L_{s}, and the portion that is transitory, L_{t}, and

the additional long-term settlements due to [REF:term:dd-ld]dead load, D, and sustained [REF:term:lv-ld]live loads, L_{s}, shall be calculated from the [REF:term:fndtn]foundation
                              [REF:term:l]soil properties provided
by a qualified professional geotechnical engineer.

body_rows.content:
Deflection for materials
not subject to creep

content.text:
In proportioning structural members to limit serviceability
problems resulting from deflections, consideration shall be given
to

clauses.text:
the intended use of the [REF:term:bldng]building or
member,

limiting damage to non-structural members made of materials
whose physical properties are known at the time of design,
limiting damage to the structure itself, and
creep, shrinkage, temperature changes and pre-stress.

content.text:
The lateral deflection of [REF:term:bldng]buildings due to service wind and gravity loads shall be checked to ensure
that structural elements and non-structural elements whose nature
is known at the time the structural design is carried out will not
be damaged.

Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art5.sent4:short], the total drift per [REF:term:tr]storey under service
wind and gravity loads shall not exceed 1/500 of the [REF:term:tr]storey height unless other drift limits are specified in the
design standards referenced in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect3:long] (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote18:short].)

The deflection limits required in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art5.sent3:short] do not apply to industrial [REF:term:bldng]buildings or sheds if experience has proven that greater movement will have
no significant adverse effects on the strength and function of the [REF:term:bldng]building.

The [REF:term:bldng]building structure shall be designed
for lateral deflection due to E, in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect8.art13:long]

Floor systems susceptible to vibration shall be designed so
that vibrations will have no significant adverse effects on the intended [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy of the [REF:term:bldng]building. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote19:short].)

Where floor vibrations caused by resonance with operating machinery
or equipment are anticipated, dynamic analysis of the floor system
shall be carried out. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote20:short].)

Where the fundamental vibration frequency of a structural system
supporting an [REF:term:mbl-ccpn]assembly occupancy used
for rhythmic activities, such as dancing, concerts, jumping exercises
or gymnastics, is less than 6 Hz (metric), the effects of resonance
shall be investigated by means of a dynamic analysis. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote21:short].)

A [REF:term:bldng]building susceptible to lateral
vibration under wind load shall be designed in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect7.art1:long] so that the vibrations will have no significant
adverse effects on the intended use and [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy of the [REF:term:bldng]building. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote22:short].)

The specified [REF:term:dd-ld]dead load for a structural
member consists of

clauses.text: the weight of the member itself,

the weight of all materials of construction incorporated into
the [REF:term:bldng]building to be supported permanently
by the member,
the weight of [REF:term:prttn]partitions,
the weight of permanent equipment, and
the vertical load due to [REF:term:l]soil, superimposed earth, plants and trees.

content.text:
In areas of a [REF:term:bldng]building for which [REF:term:prttn]partitions are shown on the drawings, the weight of [REF:term:prttn]partitions referred to in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect4.art1.sent1.clause3:medium] shall
be taken as the actual weight of such [REF:term:prttn]partitions. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote23:short].)

In areas of a [REF:term:bldng]building for which [REF:term:prttn]partitions are not shown on the drawings, the weight of [REF:term:prttn]partitions referred to in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect4.art1.sent1.clause3:medium] shall be a [REF:term:prttn]partition weight
allowance determined from the anticipated weight and position of the [REF:term:prttn]partitions, but shall not be less than 1 kPa (metric) over the area of floor being considered. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote24:short].)

The weights of [REF:term:prttn]partitions  and [REF:term:prttn]partition  weight allowances used in the design shall be shown
on the drawings as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divC.part2.sect2.subsect4.art3.sent1.clause4:long].

Where the [REF:term:prttn]partition weight allowance referred to in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect4.art1.sent3:short] is counteractive to other loads, it shall not be included in the design calculations.

Except for structures where the [REF:term:dd-ld]dead load of [REF:term:l]soil is part of the load-resisting system,
where the [REF:term:dd-ld]dead load due to [REF:term:l]soil, superimposed earth, plants and trees is counteractiveto other loads, it shall
not be included in the design calculations. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote25:short].)

subsections.title: Live Loads Due to Use and Occupancy

articles.title: Loads Due to Use of Floors and Roofs

content.text:
Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art1.sent2:short], the specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live load on an area
of floor or roof depends on the intended use and [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy, and shall not be less than either the uniformly
distributed load patterns listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art3:long], the
loads due to the intended use and [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy, or the concentrated loads listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art9:long],
whichever produces the most critical effect. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote26:short].)

For [REF:term:bldng]buildings in the Low Importance
Category as described in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect2.art1.table1:long], a factor of
0.8 may be applied to the [REF:term:lv-ld]live load.

Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art2.sent2:short], where the use of an area of floor or roof is not provided for
in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art3:long], the specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live loads due to the use and [REF:term:ccpnc]occupancy of the area shall be determined from an analysis of the loads resulting
from the weight of

clauses.text: the probable assembly of persons,
the probable accumulation of equipment and furnishings, and
the probable storage of materials.

content.text:
For [REF:term:bldng]buildings in the Low Importance
Category as described in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect2.art1.table1:long], a factor of

The uniformly distributed [REF:term:lv-ld]live load shall be not less than the value listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art3.table1:long], which may be reduced as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art8:long], applied uniformly over the entire area or on any portions of the
area, whichever produces the most critical effects in the members
concerned.

content.text:
The floor assembly and other structural elements that support
fixed seats in any [REF:term:bldng]building used for [REF:term:mbl-ccpn]assembly occupancies accommodating large numbers
of people at one time, such as grandstands, stadia and [REF:term:thtr]theatre balconies, shall be designed to resist
a horizontal force equal to not less than 0.3 kN (metric) for
each metre length of seats acting parallel to each row of seats, and
not less than 0.15 kN (metric) for each metre length of seats
acting at right angles to each row of seats, based on the assumption
that these forces are acting independently of each other.

articles.title: Crane-Supporting Structures and Impact of Machinery and Equipment

content.text:
The minimum specified load due to equipment, machinery or other
objects that may produce impact shall be the sum of the weight of
the equipment or machinery and its maximum lifting capacity, multiplied
by an appropriate factor listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art11.table1:long]

Crane-supporting structures shall be designed for the appropriate
load combinations listed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect3.art2:long]

Crane runway structures shall be designed to resist a horizontal
force applied normal to the top of the rails equal to not less than
20% of the sum of the weights of the lifted load and the crane trolley
(excluding other parts of the crane).

The force described in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art11.sent3:short] shall be equally distributed on each side of the runway and shall
be assumed to act in either direction.

Crane runway structures shall be designed to resist a horizontal
force applied parallel to the top of the rails equal to not less than
10% of the maximum wheel loads of the crane.

content.text:

metre or for a concentrated load of 2.2 kN (metric) distributed
over a length of 0.75 m (metric), whichever produces the most
critical effect on the supporting members.

Bleachers shall be checked by the erector after erection to
ensure that all structural members, including bracing specified in
the design, have been installed.

Telescopic bleachers shall be provided with locking devices
to ensure stability while in use.

Helicopter landing areas on roofs shall be constructed in conformance
with the requirements for heliports contained in [REF:standard:tc_sor433]

The minimum horizontal
specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live load applied
outward at the minimum required height of every required [REF:term:guard]guard shall be

clauses.text:
3.0 kN/m (metric) for open viewing stands without fixed
seats and for [REF:term:mn-f-gr]means of egress in grandstands,
stadia, bleachers and arenas,

1.0 kN (metric) applied at any point, so as to produce the
most critical effect, for access ways to equipment platforms, contiguous
stairs and similar areas where the gathering of many people is improbable,
and

0.75 kN/m (metric) or 1.0 kN (metric) applied at any
point so as to produce the most critical effect, whichever governs,
for locations other than those described in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent1.clause1:short]
                              [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent1.clause2:short].

content.text:
The minimum horizontal
specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live load applied
inward at the minimum required height of every required [REF:term:guard]guard shall be half that specified in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent1:short].

Individual elements within the [REF:term:guard]guard, including solid panels and pickets, shall be designed for a horizontal specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live load of 0.5 kN (metric) applied outward
over an area of 100 mm (metric) by 100 mm (metric) located
at any point on the element or elements so as to produce the most
critical effect.

The size of the opening between any two adjacent vertical elements
within a [REF:term:guard]guard shall not exceed the limits
required by Part 3 when each of these elements is subjected to a horizontal specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live load of 0.1 kN (metric) applied in opposite
directions in the in-plane direction of the [REF:term:guard]guard so as to produce the most critical effect.

The specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live loads required in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent3:short] need not be considered to act simultaneously
with the loads provided for in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent1:short]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent2:short]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent6:short]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent7:short].

The minimum specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live load applied vertically
at the top of every required [REF:term:guard]guard shall
be 1.5 kN/m (metric) and need not be considered to act simultaneously
with the horizontal specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live load provided for in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent1:short]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent3:short]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14.sent7:short].

Handrails and their supports shall be designed and constructed
to withstand the following minimum specified [REF:term:lv-ld]live loads, which need not be considered to act simultaneously:

clauses.text:
0.9 kN (metric) applied at any point and in any direction
for all handrails, and

0.7 kN/m (metric) applied in any direction for handrails
not located within [REF:term:dwllng-n]dwelling units.

content.text:
Vehicle guardrails shall be designed for a concentrated load
of 22 kN (metric) applied horizontally outward at any point 500 mm (metric) above the floor surface so as to produce the most critical
effect. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote32:short].)

The loads required in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art15.sent1:short] need not be considered to act simultaneously with the loads provided
for in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art14:long]

articles.title: Loads on Walls Acting As Guards

content.text:
Where the floor elevation on one side of a wall, including a
wall around a shaft, is more than 600 mm (metric) higher than
the elevation of the floor or ground on the other side, the wall shall
be designed to resist the appropriate outward lateral design loads
prescribed elsewhere in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5:long] or 0.5
kPa (metric) acting outward, whichever produces the more critical effect.

[REF:term:frwll]Firewalls shall be designed to resist
the maximum effect due to

clauses.text:
the appropriate lateral design loads prescribed elsewhere in
this Section, or

a factored lateral load of 0.5 kPa (metric) under fire conditions,
as described in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect5.art17.sent2:short].

content.text:
Under fire conditions, where the [REF:term:fr-rtnc-]fire-resistance
rating  of the structure is less than that of the [REF:term:frwll]firewall,

clauses.text:
lateral support shall be assumed to be provided by the structure
on one side only, or

another structural support system capable of resisting the loads
imposed by a fire on either side of the [REF:term:frwll]firewall shall be provided.

the more critical effect. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote34:short].)

the loading does not involve the accumulation of snow due to
drifting from adjacent surfaces.

content.text:
Except as provided for in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2.sent6:short]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2.sent7:short], the slope factor, C_{s}, shall be

clauses.text: 1.0 where the roof slope, α, is equal to or less than 30° (metric),

(70° − α)/40° where α is greater than 30° (metric) but not
greater than 70° (metric), and
0 where α exceeds 70° (metric).

content.title: Basic Roof Snow Load Factor for [EQ:inline:]

content.text:
The slope factor, C_{s}, for unobstructed slippery roofs
where snow and ice can slide completely off the roof shall be

clauses.text: 1.0 where the roof slope, α, is equal to or less than 15° (metric),

(60° − α)/45° where α is greater than 15° (metric) but not
greater than 60° (metric), and
0 where α exceeds 60° (metric).

content.text:
Unless otherwise stated in this Subsection, the slope factor,
C_{s}, shall be 1.0 when used in conjunction with accumulation
factors for increased snow loads.

The accumulation factor, C_{a}, shall be 1.0, which
corresponds to the uniform snow load case, except that where appropriate
for the shape of the roof, it shall be assigned other values that
account for

clauses.text:
increased non-uniform snow loads due to snow drifting onto a
roof that is at a level lower than other parts of the same [REF:term:bldng]building or at a level lower than another [REF:term:bldng]building within 5 m (metric) of it horizontally,
as prescribed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art5:long], [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art6:number]
                              [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art8:short],

increased non-uniform snow loads on areas adjacent to roof projections,
such as penthouses, large [REF:term:chmn]chimneys and equipment,
 as prescribed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art7:long]
                              [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art8:short],

non-uniform snow loads on gable, arch or curved roofs and domes,
 as prescribed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art9:long]
                              [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art10:short],

increased snow or ice loads due to snow sliding as prescribed
in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art11:long],
increased snow loads in roof valleys, as prescribed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art12:long], and
increased snow or ice loads due to meltwater draining from adjacent [REF:term:bldng]building elements and roof projections.

content.text:
For shapes not addressed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2.sent8:short], C_{a} corresponding to the non-uniform snow load case
shall be established based on applicable field observations, special
analyses including local climatic effects, appropriate model tests,
or a combination of these methods.

A roof or other [REF:term:bldng]building surface
and its structural members subject to loads due to snow accumulation
shall be designed for the specified load given in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2.sent1:long], distributed over the entire loaded area.

In addition to the distribution mentioned in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art3.sent1:short], flat roofs and shed roofs, gable
roofs of 15° (metric) slope or less, and arch or curved roofs
shall be designed for the specified uniform snow load indicated in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2.sent1:long], which shall be calculated using the accumulation
factor C_{a} = 1.0, distributed on any one portion of the
loaded area and half of this load on the remainder of the loaded area,
in such a way as to produce the most critical effects on the member
concerned. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote37:short].)

Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art4.sent4:short], the specified load, S, due to the accumulation of rainwater on
a surface whose position, shape and deflection under load make such
an accumulation possible, is that resulting from the one-day rainfall
determined in conformance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part1.sect1.subsect3:long] and
applied over the horizontal projection of the surface and all tributary
surfaces. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote38:short].)

The provisions of [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art4.sent1:short] apply
whether or not the surface is provided with a means of drainage, such
as rainwater leaders.

Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2.sent1:long], loads due
to rain need not be considered to act simultaneously with loads due
to snow. (See [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect5.appnote39:short].)

Where scuppers are provided as secondary drainage systems and where
the position, shape and deflection of the loaded surface make an accumulation
of rainwater possible, the loads due to rain shall be the lesser of
either the one-day rainfall determined in conformance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part1.sect1.subsect3:long] or a depth of rainwater equal to 30 mm (metric) above the bottom of the scuppers, applied over the horizontal projection of the
surface and tributary areas.

The drifting load of snow on a roof adjacent to a higher roof
shall be taken as trapezoidal, as shown in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art5.figure1:long], and the accumulation factor, C_{a}, shall be determined

in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art5.sent1:long] using the following
values for the peak accumulation factor, C_{a0}, and the drift
length, x_{d}:

clauses.text: C_{a0} shall be taken as the lesser of [EQ:display:eg02644b]

Where the longest horizontal dimension of the roof projection,
l_{0}, is less than 3 m (metric), the drift surcharge
adjacent to the projection need not be considered.

The drift loads on the lower level roof against the two faces
of an outside corner of an upper level roof or roof obstruction shall
be extended radially around the corner as shown in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art8.figure1:long] and may be taken as the least severe of the drift
loads lying against the two faces of the corner.

The drift loads on the lower level roof against the two faces
of an inside corner of an upper level roof or a parapet shall be calculated
for each face and the
higher of the two loads shall be applied where the drifts overlap as shown in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art8.figure2:long]

For gable roofs with a slope α > 15° (metric), the unbalanced

full and partial load cases, and
1.0 for the unbalanced load case referred to in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art9.sent2:short].

Except as provided in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art11.sent2:short], where an upper roof, or part thereof, slopes downwards with a
slope α > 0 towards a lower roof, the snow load, S, on the lower
roof, determined in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2:long]
                           [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art5:long], shall
be augmented in accordance with [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art11.sent3:short] to account for the additional load
resulting from sliding snow.
[REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art11.sent1:short] need not apply where

clauses.text:
snow from the upper roof is prevented from sliding by a parapet
or other effective means, or

the upper roof is not considered slippery and has a slope of
less than 20°.

content.text:
The total weight of additional snow resulting from sliding shall
be taken as half the total weight of snow resulting from the uniform
load case prescribed in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2:long] with

clauses.text:
the accumulation factor C_{a} = 1.0 for the relevant
part of the upper roof,

the slope factor, C_{s}, based on the slope of the lower

                              [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art2.sent6:short], and

the sliding snow distributed on the lower roof such that it
is a maximum for x = 0 (metric) and decreases linearly to 0 at x = xd
                               (metric), as shown in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art11.figure1:long], where x and x_{d} are as defined in [REF:internal:nbc.divB.part4.sect1.subsect6.art5:long]

content.title: Snow loads in valleys of sloped or curved roofs
